# CyberTalents Arson Challenge Writeup
> CyberTalents has a few neat PCAP CTFs for us to solve

We have a pretty big PCAP and we know a malicious script was executed. I started simply scrolling through the pcap to see if I notice anything odd straight away. So the stuff I point out won’t necessarily lead to the solution.  
I saw weird UDP communication from the same source to destination port, **54915**, to a broadcast. Following this stream we see a randomized type 4 GUID and a hostname:  
![][image1]  
Then I saw an HTTP get request for a powershell file, ok this is probably it :)  
![][image2]  
Following the HTTP stream we’ll be able to see the entire script:

"razer"$sleep\_time \= 5First $key $ip $port $implant\_nameExecute $key $ip $port $implant\_name $sleep\_time ```

It’s a pretty long script but let’s try to go through it.  
First of all the data is encrypted with AES, and thankfully we have most of our variables to decrypt it later:

* Key \- llm0xB8WOfv9Ssq9+f0sIMFK6OyQHOzhdenMzRInqXA=

The first function being executed is First, let’s follow it:  
The function received 4 arguments:  
$key \= "llm0xB8WOfv9Ssq9+f0sIMFK6OyQHOzhdenMzRInqXA="  
$ip \= "192.168.1.11"  
$port \= "7788"  
$implant\_name \= "razer"

Then it gathers up the Hostname, username and LocalIps of the machine and encrypts them using the key mentioned above, then it sends out the HTTP POST packet with this exact data.  
It encrypts the data in a different function:  
```
function Encrypt-String($key, $unencryptedString) {  
$bytes \= \[System.Text.Encoding\]::UTF8.GetBytes($unencryptedString)  
$aesManaged \= Create-AesManagedObject $key  
$encryptor \= $aesManaged.CreateEncryptor()  
$encryptedData \= $encryptor.TransformFinalBlock($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length);  
\[byte\[\]\] $fullData \= $aesManaged.IV \+ $encryptedData  
$aesManaged.Dispose()  
\[System.Convert\]::ToBase64String($fullData)  
}
```
First the string data is encoded into bytes, then it encrypts using AES and the key.  
We also see the function which decrypts the data:  
![][image3]  
The encrypted data is in base64, so it is converted to hex, then we find our IV \- the first 16 bytes of the encrypted data, from here it is easy to decrypt in cyberchef:  
![][image4]  
We find that:

* Machine Name: t3st3r  
* Username: SEC401-Student  
* Local IP: 192.168.1.4

This way we can also decrypt other encrypted POST packets sent:  
![][image5]  
In one of these, we’ll find the flag:  
![][image6]
